episodes.title: Why Your Card Wants You to Pay the Minimum
episodes.hook: Why does your credit card company want you to pay the minimum?
episodes.twist: On $3,000 at about 22% APR, a minimum of interest plus 1% takes 15 years and about $4,400 in interest; the payoff box is printed on your statement by law.
sources: Federal Reserve, G.19 Consumer Credit release: interest rate on credit card plans, accounts assessed interest (about 22% through 2025)
CFPB, Regulation Z 12 CFR 1026.7(b)(12): the minimum payment warning and repayment disclosures required on every statement (Credit CARD Act of 2009)

episodes.title: Why Your Gym Hopes You Never Show Up
episodes.hook: Your gym is counting on you NOT coming.
episodes.twist: Members paying over $70 a month went about 4.3 times a month: over $17 a visit, when a 10-visit pass cost $10 a visit. Gyms sell far more memberships than they have room for.
sources: DellaVigna & Malmendier, 'Paying Not to Go to the Gym', American Economic Review 96(3), 2006
U.S. Federal Trade Commission, 'Bringing Dark Patterns to Light' staff report, September 2022 (hard-to-cancel subscriptions)

episodes.title: The Rule of 72: When Your Money Doubles
episodes.hook: There's one number that tells you when your money doubles.
episodes.twist: Divide 72 by the yearly rate: at 6% it doubles in about 12 years, at 9% about 8. It works on debt too: 24% credit card debt doubles in about 3 years.
sources: U.S. SEC, Investor.gov glossary: 'Rule of 72'
Brealey, Myers & Allen, Principles of Corporate Finance (McGraw-Hill), chapter on compound interest and present value

episodes.title: Why Prices End in .99
episodes.hook: $4.99 is basically $5. So why does your brain read it as $4?
episodes.twist: The left-digit effect: we read prices left to right and anchor on the first digit. In a field test, dresses sold more at $39 than at $34.
sources: Thomas & Morwitz, 'Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left-Digit Effect in Price Cognition', Journal of Consumer Research, 2005
Anderson & Simester, 'Effects of $9 Price Endings on Retail Sales: Evidence from Field Experiments', Quantitative Marketing and Economics, 2003

episodes.title: How 'Pay in 4' Makes Money With 0% Interest
episodes.hook: Buy now, pay later charges you zero interest. So who's paying?
episodes.twist: The store pays: merchant fees are often several times a card fee, because shoppers spend more. Plus late fees, and many users juggle several loans at once.
sources: CFPB, 'Buy Now, Pay Later: Market trends and consumer impacts', September 2022
CFPB, 'Consumer Use of Buy Now, Pay Later and Other Unsecured Debt', January 2025

episodes.title: Inflation, Explained With a Candy Bar
episodes.hook: Your candy bar didn't get more expensive. Your dollar got weaker.
episodes.twist: At the Fed's 2% target, prices double in about 36 years (rule of 72); at 8%, as in mid-2022, in about 9.
sources: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index (CPI-U, 12-month change peaked at 9.1% in June 2022)
Federal Reserve, 'Why does the Federal Reserve aim for inflation of 2 percent over the longer run?' (FAQ)

episodes.title: Shrinkflation: Same Price, Less Snack
episodes.hook: The price didn't go up. So why are you getting less?
episodes.twist: Companies shrink the pack instead of raising the price, because we notice prices and not grams. Statisticians catch it by tracking price per unit.
sources: UK Office for National Statistics, 'The shrinking size of the nation's chocolate bars' / shrinkflation analysis, 2017 (2,529 products shrank 2012-2017)
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 'Product downsizing (shrinkflation)' in the CPI

episodes.title: How 'Free' Trading Apps Make Money
episodes.hook: Zero-commission trading. So how is the app making billions?
episodes.twist: Payment for order flow: the app sends your order to a market maker who pays for it. The SEC fined Robinhood $65 million in 2020 for misleading customers about it.
sources: U.S. SEC, 'Staff Report on Equity and Options Market Structure Conditions in Early 2021', October 2021
U.S. SEC press release 2020-321, 'SEC Charges Robinhood Financial With Misleading Customers', December 2020

episodes.title: The Secret Recipe of Your Credit Score
episodes.hook: Your credit score isn't a grade. It's a recipe, and you can read it.
episodes.twist: 35% payment history, 30% amounts owed, 15% length of history, 10% new credit, 10% credit mix. Checking your own score doesn't lower it.
sources: myFICO (Fair Isaac), 'What's in my FICO Scores?'
CFPB, 'What is a credit score?' and 'Does checking my credit report hurt my score?'

episodes.title: The Free Trial Is the Product
episodes.hook: That free trial isn't free. It's a bet that you'll forget.
episodes.twist: Auto-renewal plus a hard cancel button is a known 'dark pattern'; regulators have gone after it, and the business still relies on people who forget.
sources: U.S. Federal Trade Commission, 'Bringing Dark Patterns to Light', staff report, September 2022
U.S. Federal Trade Commission, press release on the Negative Option ('click to cancel') rule, October 2024 (later vacated by the 8th Circuit, July 2025)

episodes.title: How Airlines Earn Billions From Free Miles
episodes.hook: How does an airline earn billions from miles it gives away?
episodes.twist: Banks buy miles to hand out on credit cards: Delta reported about $7 billion a year from American Express. The airline decides what a mile is worth, and can change it.
sources: Delta Air Lines, Form 10-K for 2024 (SEC EDGAR), American Express remuneration
U.S. Department of Transportation, inquiry into airline rewards programs, press release September 2024

episodes.title: Why Your Bank Pays You Almost Nothing
episodes.hook: Your bank lends your money out at a high rate, and pays you almost nothing for it.
episodes.twist: The gap is the net interest margin, the bank's main business. Rates on savings accounts vary hugely between banks, and the bank isn't going to tell you.
sources: FDIC, National Rates and Rate Caps (national average savings rate)
Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED), 'Net Interest Margin for all U.S. Banks'

episodes.title: Banks Don't Lend Your Savings. They Create Money
episodes.hook: Everyone thinks banks lend out your savings. They don't even need them.
episodes.twist: When a bank makes a loan it creates a new deposit: most money in the economy is created that way, by commercial banks, not printed.
sources: Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin 2014 Q1, 'Money creation in the modern economy' (McLeay, Radia & Thomas)
Bank of England, 'How is money created?' (Knowledge Bank explainer)

episodes.title: What Is a Dollar Actually Worth?
episodes.hook: Your dollar isn't backed by gold. So why does it work?
episodes.twist: Since 1971 the dollar can't be swapped for gold: it works because everyone, including the government that takes taxes in it, agrees it does.
sources: Federal Reserve History, 'Nixon Ends Convertibility of U.S. Dollars to Gold and Announces Wage/Price Controls' (August 1971)
Federal Reserve Board FAQ, 'Is U.S. currency still backed by gold?'

episodes.title: The Penny That Cost Almost 4 Cents
episodes.hook: This penny cost almost four cents to make.
episodes.twist: In fiscal 2024 each penny cost 3.69 cents to make and ship, the 19th year above face value; the U.S. struck its last circulating penny in November 2025. Penny takes it personally.
sources: United States Mint, 2024 Annual Report (unit cost of the one-cent coin: 3.69 cents)
U.S. Department of the Treasury / United States Mint announcements on ending penny production, 2025

episodes.title: Why Stores Give You a Loyalty Card
episodes.hook: That loyalty card isn't about your discount. It's about your data.
episodes.twist: Every scan tells the store what you buy, when and for how much; regulators are now studying 'surveillance pricing', where prices can follow your profile.
sources: U.S. Federal Trade Commission, 'Surveillance pricing' 6(b) study, initial staff findings, January 2025
U.S. Federal Trade Commission, 'Data Brokers: A Call for Transparency and Accountability', May 2014 (purchase data collected and sold)

episodes.title: How Insurance Companies Get Rich
episodes.hook: Insurance companies get paid before anything goes wrong. That's the trick.
episodes.twist: Premiums come in now, claims go out later: the money in between ('float') gets invested. Berkshire Hathaway built an empire on it.
sources: Berkshire Hathaway, annual shareholder letters (Warren Buffett on insurance float)
Insurance Information Institute (III), 'Facts + Statistics: Industry overview' (premiums, claims and investment income)

episodes.title: The $34 Coffee: Overdraft Fees
episodes.hook: Your bank charged you $34 for a $24 coffee run. As a loan, that's a 17,000% rate.
episodes.twist: The CFPB's math: borrow $24 for 3 days, pay a $34 fee, and the yearly rate works out to about 17,000%. Small amounts plus short times make APRs explode.
sources: CFPB, 'Data Point: Checking Account Overdraft', July 2014, and press release 'CFPB Finds Small Debit Purchases Lead to Expensive Overdraft Charges'
CNN Money, '17,000% interest? Small purchases trigger big overdraft fees', July 31, 2014

episodes.title: The Lottery Jackpot Isn't What You Win
episodes.hook: The jackpot says a billion. You'd never see a billion.
episodes.twist: The headline is the 30-year annuity; the cash option is much smaller, then 24% federal withholding comes off. Odds of the Powerball jackpot: 1 in 292,201,338.
sources: Powerball official site (Multi-State Lottery Association), 'Prizes and odds' and 'Annuity vs cash option'
Internal Revenue Service, Publication 505 / gambling winnings withholding at 24% (Form W-2G instructions)

episodes.title: Why the Cashier Pushes the Extended Warranty
episodes.hook: Why does the cashier care so much about your warranty?
episodes.twist: Extended warranties are among the most profitable things a store sells, because most products never break during the cover period, and many are already covered by the maker's warranty.
sources: U.S. Federal Trade Commission, 'Warranties' and 'Extended warranties and service contracts' consumer guidance
Consumer Reports, reporting on extended warranties and product repair rates
